question: Can a small network copy the cheating script well enough to do the pick and place itself?
measure: Two things. Offline: how closely the network's commands match the script's on the recorded rows (mean squared error, MSE, and the largest single error). Closed loop: successes out of 3 when the network drives the arm in the simulator.
outcome: It copied the script to the memorization bar (MSE 9.999720305e-07) and then failed all 3 tries, lifting the cube 0.0001588361 m (about 0.16 mm). Small errors pile up until the arm is somewhere the recording never went.
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. The teacher here is the privileged controller from experiment 01: a script that cheats by reading the cube's true position. Behaviour cloning means recording the teacher and training a network to output the same command from the same state. The recording is one episode of 450 steps (rows). The network is a small MLP (a plain stack of fully connected layers) that sees joint positions, the cube's position and a progress clock (10 inputs). "ACT units" are the motor-range units the commands are stored in. The offline gate, set beforehand, is near-exact memorization: MSE at most 1e-6 and largest error at most 0.01 ACT. Closed loop means the network's own commands move the arm, so its next input depends on its last output. Offline means comparing against the recording only.

parts.title: Do the old policies work on the fixed simulator?
parts.why: If any older policy works now that the simulator is fixed, there is no need to start again.
parts.did: Re-ran every older policy (current-pose, mean, state-only, image-state and black-image) on the proven simulator.
parts.conclusion: 165 matched rollouts: every old policy had zero reach, contact and success. The selected comparison clipped or limited its commands on a 0.9148148148 share of frames.

parts.title: Can the network memorize the 450 rows?
parts.why: If it cannot even reproduce the recording, there is no point letting it drive.
parts.did: Trained the MLP on the 450 rows. Each change was one step: a smoother teacher retreat, width 128 to 256, then a learning-rate schedule (1e-3, 1e-4, 1e-5).

predictions.text: Offline gate set beforehand: normalized MSE at most 1e-6 and largest error at most 0.01 ACT on all 450 rows

parts.conclusion: It took a wider network and a decaying learning rate, but the copy reached the bar with zero unsafe commands on the training rows.

parts.title: Does the memorized copy work when it drives?
parts.why: This is the real test. A copy that is exact on the recording may still fail once its own small errors change what it sees.
parts.did: Ran the one authorized evaluation: 3 repeats from the normal start in MuJoCo.

cells: the clone's commands replayed on the teacher's states

parts.conclusion: The copy failed every try without ever grasping. The first command error is at action 0. Joint error passes 0.005 ACT by action 31 and 0.01 by action 74. Both arms first touch the cube at action 194, where the cube positions split by about 0.0209 mm. But when the clone's 450 commands were computed on the teacher's recorded states and replayed, the full pick and place succeeded. So the outputs are good enough; the drift is the problem. This is called covariate shift.

trust.text: All three closed-loop repeats were deterministic and identical.
The fixed-action replay isolates the cause: same network, same commands, only the feedback loop removed.
One training seed, one start position, one recorded episode.
The log says the joints are "half a degree off" by step 74. The source gives 0.01 ACT units, not degrees. The ACT figure is used here.
Simulation only, with privileged inputs (the cube's true position) that a real arm does not have.

meaning: The pipeline from teacher to network works, but near-exact memorization does not predict closed-loop success. The rebuild plan later retired the 1e-6 gate as "proven non-predictive". The next experiments try to teach recovery: a few recovery examples (03, 04), more inputs (05), then corrections from the clone's own mistakes (06).
lesson: A perfect fit on training data says nothing about what happens once the model's own mistakes change its inputs. A policy that only copied a perfect path has never seen a mistake, so it cannot fix one.

next.title: Add a few recovery examples (experiment 03)
next.why: The clone drifts and has never seen how to get back.

next.title: Give it more inputs (experiment 05)
next.why: It sees no velocities or contact, so it may not be able to tell where it is.

log:
**TL;DR:** A network copied the script almost perfectly on paper, then failed
every real try, because tiny errors piled up until the arm was somewhere new.

**Problem.** After entry 01 the task was solvable, but only by a script that
cheats. I needed a learned policy, and the old ones were useless.

*How we know:* I re-ran every older policy on the fixed sim, 165 rollouts total,
and none of them even reached the cube. I didn't know if learning could work
here at all.

**Experiment.** Behaviour cloning, basically copying an expert: record the
script once (450 steps), train a small MLP to output the same command from the
same state until it's almost exact, then let it drive the arm 3 times.

*What we hope to learn:* if a near-perfect copy succeeds, the pipeline works and
I can scale up. If it fails, I need to know why.

**Outcome.** It hit the "basically memorized" bar (training error under 1e-6)
and still failed all 3 tries, lifting the cube 0.16 mm:

- Small errors compound. The copy is off by a hair every step, and by step 74
  its joints are half a degree off. Think of a steering wheel that's slightly
  off: fine for a second, in a ditch after a mile.
- Off the recording, it's guessing. It only saw states the script visited, so
  at contact it's somewhere new and never closes on the cube. Like memorizing an
  answer key and then getting a question with one number changed.

To prove it, I fed the network the script's exact recorded states and replayed
its commands: full pick and place. The outputs were fine. The drift was the
problem.

**Takeaway:** a perfect fit on training data says nothing about what happens
once the model's own mistakes change its inputs (called covariate shift). A
policy that only copied a perfect path has never seen a mistake, so it can't
fix one.
